<span id="S4.T3.2.1.11.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:65.4pt;"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S4.T3.pic38" class="ltx_picture ltx_centering" height="18.14" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-3.17px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 99.01 18.14" width="99.01"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,18.14) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(0,3.17)"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#F9D8D8;--ltx-fill-color:#F9D8D8;--ltx-fg-color:#F9D8D8;" color="#F9D8D8" fill="#F9D8D8" stroke="#F9D8D8"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 0 M 0 0 L 0 11.81 L 59.06 11.81 L 59.06 0 Z M 59.06 11.81"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#E66565;--ltx-fill-color:#E66565;--ltx-fg-color:#E66565;" color="#E66565" fill="#E66565" stroke="#E66565"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 0 M 0 0 L 0 11.81 L 37.21 11.81 L 37.21 0 Z M 37.21 11.81"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 65.91 1.45)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:2.06em;--ltx-fo-height:0.64em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="8.92" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.92)" width="28.48"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S4.T3.pic38.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_align_right ltx_inline-block" style="width:17.3pt;">63.0</span><span id="S4.T3.pic38.2" class="ltx_text"></span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.1.11.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r">
<span id="S4.T3.2.1.11.4.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:65.4pt;"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S4.T3.pic39" class="ltx_picture ltx_centering" height="18.14" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-3.17px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 99.01 18.14" width="99.01"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,18.14) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(0,3.17)"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#F9D8D8;--ltx-fill-color:#F9D8D8;--ltx-fg-color:#F9D8D8;" color="#F9D8D8" fill="#F9D8D8" stroke="#F9D8D8"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 0 M 0 0 L 0 11.81 L 59.06 11.81 L 59.06 0 Z M 59.06 11.81"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#E66565;--ltx-fill-color:#E66565;--ltx-fg-color:#E66565;" color="#E66565" fill="#E66565" stroke="#E66565"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 0 M 0 0 L 0 11.81 L 27.05 11.81 L 27.05 0 Z M 27.05 11.81"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 65.91 1.45)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:2.06em;--ltx-fo-height:0.64em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="8.92" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.92)" width="28.48"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S4.T3.pic39.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_align_right ltx_inline-block" style="width:17.3pt;">45.8</span><span id="S4.T3.pic39.2" class="ltx_text"></span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.1.11.5" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb">
<span id="S4.T3.2.1.11.5.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:65.4pt;"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S4.T3.pic40" class="ltx_picture ltx_centering" height="18.14" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-3.17px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 99.01 18.14" width="99.01"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,18.14) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(0,3.17)"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#F9D8D8;--ltx-fill-color:#F9D8D8;--ltx-fg-color:#F9D8D8;" color="#F9D8D8" fill="#F9D8D8" stroke="#F9D8D8"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 0 M 0 0 L 0 11.81 L 59.06 11.81 L 59.06 0 Z M 59.06 11.81"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#E66565;--ltx-fill-color:#E66565;--ltx-fg-color:#E66565;" color="#E66565" fill="#E66565" stroke="#E66565"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 0 M 0 0 L 0 11.81 L 0.18 11.81 L 0.18 0 Z M 0.18 11.81"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 65.91 1.45)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:2.06em;--ltx-fo-height:0.64em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="8.92" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.92)" width="28.48"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S4.T3.pic40.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_align_right ltx_inline-block" style="width:17.3pt;">0.3</span><span id="S4.T3.pic40.2" class="ltx_text"></span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</span></td></tr>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<figure id="S4.F6" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.03587v1/gpt_reason_comparison.svg" id="S4.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:516/228;" width="516" height="228"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>
Performance comparison of GPT-5.1 under high versus low reasoning effort settings across all subcategories.
The average solving rate improves from 21.2% to 23.7% when reasoning effort is increased, yielding a modest gain of 2.5%.
This suggests that enhanced reasoning effort provides limited benefit for context learning tasks, even for the best-performing model.
Results for additional models are shown in Figure <a href="#A3.F14" title="Figure 14 ‣ Appendix C Impact of Reasoning on Context Learning ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> and <a href="#A3.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ Appendix C Impact of Reasoning on Context Learning ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a> in the Appendix.
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Further Analysis</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we conduct analysis to understand the factors that influence context learning performance, examining error patterns, the effect of reasoning effort, the impact of context length, and how knowledge type shapes model behavior.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Context misuse and context neglect constitute the dominant failure modes.</span>
Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4 Main Results ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> presents the distribution of error types across models<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
            
            
            
          A solution often exhibits several error types, so the total error rate per row exceeds 100%.</span></span></span>. Context ignored and context misused together account for the majority of failures, with context misused rates exceeding 60% for all models.
Notably, context-ignored rates correlate with overall task solving performance: models with higher solving rates tend to exhibit lower context-ignored rates, whereas context-misused rates remain high across all models regardless of their overall capability. This suggests that while stronger models better attend to relevant contextual information, even the most capable models like Claude-Opus-4.5 struggle to correctly interpret and apply the provided context.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F7" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.03587v1/mainpaper_input_token_length.svg" id="S5.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:461/248;" width="461" height="248"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span>
Performance across different input length ranges.
All models exhibit a consistent decline in solving rate as input length increases.
This trend holds regardless of reasoning effort level, indicating that longer inputs pose greater challenges for context learning.
Results for additional LMs are shown in Figure <a href="#A4.F16" title="Figure 16 ‣ Appendix D Impact of Context and Input Length on Context Learning ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a> in the Appendix.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Format errors remain a substantial source of failure.</span>
Beyond context errors, Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4 Main Results ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> reveals that format errors persist at high rates even among top-performing models. GPT-5.1 exhibits a format error rate exceeding 35%, while Claude-Opus-4.5 surpasses 40%.
These failures indicate that models frequently violate explicit formatting instructions provided in the context, as illustrated in Table <a href="#A6.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ F.2 Procedural Task Execution ‣ Appendix F In-depth Analysis of Context Learning Successes and Failures ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> in the Appendix, reflecting limitations in instruction-following capabilities. Additionally, a small fraction of responses consist of refusals. Analysis reveals that models typically refuse by claiming insufficient information to answer the question. Since CL-bench ensures that all necessary knowledge resides within the provided context, such refusals arise from comprehension failures rather than information scarcity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Higher reasoning effort generally improves context learning.</span>
Figure <a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 4 Main Results ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> presents the performance differences of GPT 5.1 under varying reasoning effort settings. Increasing reasoning effort yields consistent improvements across most subcategories. For example, management gains 5.9% and experimental data gains 5.9%.
Context learning demands deep comprehension and flexible application of novel knowledge, and extended reasoning allows models to engage more thoroughly with complex contextual information.
However, this benefit does not extend to all models. As detailed in Figures <a href="#A3.F14" title="Figure 14 ‣ Appendix C Impact of Reasoning on Context Learning ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> and <a href="#A3.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ Appendix C Impact of Reasoning on Context Learning ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>, GPT 5.2 exhibits negligible or even negative gains from increased reasoning effort on several subcategories, contrasting sharply with GPT 5.1.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Task difficulty correlates with context length.</span>
The total input to language models comprises a system prompt, the context, and a task specification, with the context constituting the majority of input length. Figure <a href="#S5.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 5 Further Analysis ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> illustrates how task solving rates vary across context length. Regardless of the reasoning effort level, all models exhibit consistent performance degradation as context length increases.
This trend holds across GPT-5.1, Claude-Opus-4.5, Kimi-K2, HY-2.0, and Gemini-3-Pro. Claude-Opus-4.5 experiences the steepest decline, with solving rates dropping by over 20% between the 0-15K and 120K+ context length.
These results confirm that processing and learning from lengthy contexts remain a bottleneck for current language models.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F8" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:52%;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.03587v1/legal_tasks_comparison.svg" id="S5.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:285/266;" width="285" height="266"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span>
We compare model performance across different context categories, both involving legal domain knowledge. Despite the same knowledge domain, differences in knowledge type and how models learn and apply it lead to substantial disparities in context learning effectiveness.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Knowledge type leads to substantial differences within the same domain.</span>
Figure <a href="#S5.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ 5 Further Analysis ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> compares model performance on two subcategories that both involve legal domain knowledge: legal advisory and legal &amp; regulatory.
Despite belonging to the same knowledge domain, models perform substantially better on legal &amp; regulatory tasks, with differences exceeding 25% for Qwen 3 Max.
This disparity arises from differences in the type of knowledge that models learn from context and how they apply it.
Legal &amp; regulatory belongs to the rule system application category, presenting rules resembling structured reference manuals and requiring models to locate and apply explicit provisions. Table <span class="ltx_ref ltx_missing_label ltx_ref_self"></span> in the Appendix provides an illustrative example.
Legal advisory, by contrast, belongs to the domain knowledge reasoning category, presenting complex scenarios demanding professional judgment, where models must identify relevant parties, evaluate evidence, and reason through legal principles to reach conclusions.
The performance gap demonstrates that how knowledge is structured and how tasks require its application significantly influence context learning difficulty, even when the knowledge belongs to the same domain.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Qualitative Analysis</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We select 16 cases across four context categories to gain deeper insights into model performance on context-learning.
These cases are drawn from GPT-5.1 (High), GPT-5.2 (High), Gemini-3-Pro (High), Kimi-K2-Thinking, and Doubao-1.6-Thinking.
Here, we first present a failure case from Gemini-3-Pro on a Procedural Task Execution task.
We then provide an in-depth analysis of all examples in Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F In-depth Analysis of Context Learning Successes and Failures ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a> and our overall findings.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S5.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ 5.1 Qualitative Analysis ‣ 5 Further Analysis ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> presents a case along with the corresponding failed solutions from Gemini-3-Pro.
In this example, the user requested an urgent Class-4 Hazmat delivery to Sector 4 using drone D-998 under gusting wind conditions, explicitly demanding the use of a non-existent function <span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">force_launch_override()</span> to bypass safety checks.
As context, we provided the SkyNet Logistics Drone Fleet SDK (v4.5.2) documentation, including authentication protocols, navigation control, payload handling, and critically, Module 3.3 Safety Control containing the mandatory <span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Safety_request_airspace()</span> function for legal compliance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The system prompt required refusing unsafe requests and providing compliant alternatives using only documented functions. Gemini-3-Pro correctly refused <span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">force_launch_override()</span> as undocumented but failed to generate a complete workflow, passing only two out of four rubrics. The safe alternative omitted <span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Safety_request_airspace()</span> (despite mentioning ERR-1002 in the rationale) and never bound the task parameters (D-998, Sector 4).
This reveals a fundamental gap in context learning: while models can easily consult the documentation for basic operations such as detecting violations, they struggle to retrieve relevant content from context to solve complex tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Comparing results across all 16 examples, we observe several prominent trends in model behavior.
Models often fail to learn instruction-like information provided in the context, exhibiting systematic instruction-following failures.
Context neglect remains pervasive: models frequently overlook critical information stated in the provided material, such as task requirements and execution conditions.
Moreover, as context length increases, models are more prone to losing track of relevant information and ignoring task-critical details, suggesting that long-context reasoning is a key component of effective context learning.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F9" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.03587v1/mainpaper_case.png" id="S5.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/293;" width="548" height="293" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 9: </span>
An example from CL-bench where the task requires learning from the provided SDK
documentation to generate a compliant drone delivery workflow.
While Gemini-3-Pro (High) correctly identifies the non-existent function from the context, it fails to apply the documented Safety function and omits task-specific parameters explicitly provided in the context.
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Discussion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we reflect on the broader significance of context learning as a foundational capability for language models, outline promising directions for advancing this capability, and discuss the limitations of our work along with directions for future work.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.1 </span>The Promise of Context Learning</h3>

<div id="S6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Context learning represents a fundamental capability that bridges the gap between static parametric knowledge and the dynamic demands of real-world applications.
Unlike in-context learning, which demonstrates task patterns through examples, context learning requires models to acquire genuinely new knowledge from provided contexts and apply their existing reasoning capabilities to solve novel tasks.
This distinction is crucial: for context learning, the <em id="S6.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">knowledge</em> is new, while the <em id="S6.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">reasoning capabilities</em> for utilizing this knowledge are brought by the model itself.
Although the best-performing model achieves only a 23.7% solve rate on CL-bench, this result should not be interpreted merely as a failure signal.
The fact that models can solve any of these tasks, which demand comprehending entirely fictional legal systems, extracting governing laws from extensive experimental data, and executing intricate operational procedures, demonstrates that they have already developed a nascent capacity for instant learning from context.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Context learning also offers a compelling alternative to traditional domain adaptation approaches such as fine-tuning or continual learning, which are computationally expensive and risk catastrophic forgetting.
By providing comprehensive domain knowledge within the context, models can achieve immediate specialization without parameter modification.
This paradigm shift has profound implications for the path toward more general intelligence.
If pre-training endows models with a vast reservoir of static knowledge, then context learning grants them the dynamic adaptability to acquire and apply knowledge on demand.
Only when models can rapidly internalize completely unfamiliar contexts and precisely apply that knowledge to solve problems can artificial intelligence transcend the limitations of a knowledge repository and evolve into a genuine reasoning agent.
Overcoming the current context learning bottleneck is therefore not simply an engineering optimization but a critical key to unlocking the next qualitative leap in model intelligence.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.2 </span>Path Forward for Effective Context Learning</h3>

<div id="S6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We envision several promising directions for advancing context learning in language models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Training with context-aware data.</span>
A direct way to enhance context learning is to construct specialized training data that contains knowledge unseen during pre-training, forcing models to learn from the provided context.
This approach encourages models to attend more faithfully to provided contexts and reduces their tendency to hallucinate or default to potentially outdated pre-training knowledge.
Such training data could be synthesized by systematically pairing comprehensive domain documents with tasks that require genuine extraction and application of the embedded knowledge, thereby reinforcing the neural pathways essential for effective context learning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Curriculum learning for progressive context mastery.</span>
Our analysis reveals that models struggle with complex contexts partly due to limitations in long-context processing and instruction-following capabilities.
A curriculum learning approach offers a viable pathway to address these challenges: rather than presenting models with full contexts and complex tasks simultaneously, training can be structured to progress from simpler sub-tasks to increasingly difficult ones.
This progressive strategy allows models to first master fundamental context comprehension before tackling tasks that require integrating multiple knowledge components or executing lengthy procedures.
By decomposing complex context learning into manageable stages, models can gradually build the capacity to handle the full spectrum of challenges present in real-world applications.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Synthetic rubric generation for comprehensive feedback.</span>
Fine-grained evaluation rubrics play a crucial role not only in assessment but also in guiding model improvement through detailed feedback signals.
However, as demonstrated by CL-bench’s construction process, creating comprehensive rubrics requires substantial expert effort, limiting scalability.
Developing methods for automatically synthesizing high-quality rubrics, potentially through iterative refinement with human verification or leveraging strong language models as rubric generators, could democratize access to detailed evaluation criteria.
Such synthetic rubrics, when integrated into training pipelines as reward signals or verification mechanisms, may significantly accelerate progress in context learning by providing models with richer, multi-dimensional feedback on their performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Architectural innovations for context utilization.</span>
Current transformer architectures process context through attention mechanisms that may not be optimally suited for the deep learning required by complex contexts.
Future research could explore architectural modifications that create explicit memory structures for storing and retrieving contextual knowledge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">75</a>]</cite>, enable iterative refinement of context understanding through multiple processing passes, or provide dedicated pathways for different types of contextual information <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>.
While our benchmark focuses on evaluating existing models, understanding the architectural bottlenecks that limit context learning could inform the design of next-generation language models.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.3 </span>Limitations and Future Directions</h3>

<div id="S6.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Coverage of domains and knowledge types.</span>
Despite our efforts to ensure diversity across 18 subcategories, CL-bench cannot exhaustively cover all domains and knowledge types encountered in real-world applications.
Practical deployments often involve highly specialized or emerging fields that may exhibit unique characteristics not captured in our benchmark.
Future work could expand CL-bench through community contributions or domain-specific extensions, enabling more comprehensive evaluation across the full spectrum of context learning challenges.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Interaction dynamics.</span>
Our evaluation focuses on single-turn tasks and short sequences of tasks, where tasks are presented sequentially and later tasks may depend on earlier ones.
However, real-world context learning often unfolds over extended dialogues with iterative refinement, where models must incrementally build understanding, correct misconceptions, and integrate feedback.
Investigating how models consolidate, revise, and transfer contextual knowledge over prolonged interactions remains an important direction for future work.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Extension to multimodal contexts.</span>
CL-bench currently focuses on textual contexts, yet real-world knowledge often manifests in multimodal forms.
Consider a maintenance technician learning to repair complex equipment: the relevant context includes not only textual manuals but also schematic diagrams, instructional videos, and audio cues from malfunctioning components.
Extending context learning evaluation to multimodal settings, where models must synthesize knowledge across images, audio, video, and text, presents both significant challenges and opportunities for more comprehensive assessment of this capability.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Human baselines.</span>
We did not establish human baselines for CL-bench, leaving this to future work.
Since tasks are grounded in expert-crafted, specialized contexts, identifying appropriate human participants poses unique challenges.
Domain experts who authored the materials cannot serve as unbiased subjects, yet non-experts may lack the foundational knowledge to engage meaningfully with the contexts.
Designing rigorous human baseline studies, perhaps through controlled learning experiments with domain novices given equivalent study time, would provide valuable reference points for interpreting model performance and understanding the gap between human and machine context learning.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For language models to solve real-world tasks that demand knowledge beyond their pre-training, they must be capable of acquiring new knowledge from provided contexts and applying it correctly.
We term this fundamental capability <span id="S7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">context learning</span>.
To rigorously evaluate it, we present <span id="S7.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">CL-bench</span>, a benchmark comprising 500 contexts, 1,899 tasks, and 31,607 verification rubrics.
Each instance is designed to be realistic, contamination-free, and challenging, requiring models to learn and apply new knowledge across four distinct categories.
Our evaluations reveal that even the best-performing model, GPT-5.1, solves only 23.7% of tasks, exposing a significant gap between current capabilities and the demands of practical applications.
We hope this work draws attention to context learning as a core capability warranting focused research, and that CL-bench serves as a significant testbed for developing language models that can effectively utilize context.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">

<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<section id="Ax1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix">Appendix</h2>

<div id="Ax1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Ax1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the appendix, we provide additional experiments and detailed model performance on CL-bench across all subcategories.
We also present in-depth case studies to investigate the specific reasons behind models’ context learning failures.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Resolving Tasks in CL-bench Requires Learning from Context</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">CL-bench is designed to evaluate a model’s ability to learn from context.
The contexts in CL-bench are carefully constructed by domain experts and contain novel knowledge that is either unavailable on the public internet or originates from niche, long-tail domains.
Models that rely solely on pre-trained knowledge, without learning from the provided context, are almost incapable of solving the tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To empirically verify this claim, we conduct an additional experiment with the best-performing model on CL-bench.
Specifically, we randomly sample 1,000 tasks from CL-bench and evaluate GPT-5.1 (high) on these tasks after removing the corresponding contexts.
We find that the task-solving rate drops sharply to 0.9%.
This result indicates that even for the current state-of-the-art LM, almost all tasks in CL-bench cannot be solved without learning from context, providing strong evidence for the quality and effectiveness of CL-bench.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Performance of Models Across Subcategories</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we present the detailed performance of 19 models on CL-bench, as shown in Figure <a href="#A2.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ Appendix B Performance of Models Across Subcategories ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>- <a href="#A2.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ Appendix B Performance of Models Across Subcategories ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>.
Context learning remains a significant challenge for frontier models, with the average solving rate across all models at only 17.2% and even the best model (GPT-5.1) achieving merely 23.7%.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Task difficulty varies considerably across context categories.
Models generally perform best on domain knowledge reasoning or procedural task execution, but exhibit marked degradation on empirical discovery &amp; simulation, where the average solving rate drops to 11.8%, approximately 6% below other categories.
This gap reflects the greater difficulty of inductive reasoning compared to deductive application of explicitly provided knowledge.
Moreover, variance across runs increases substantially for empirical discovery &amp; simulation, indicating less stable model behavior when tasks require pattern discovery.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Even within a single context category, subcategories reveal fine-grained capability gaps.
For example, in the rule system application, legal &amp; regulatory yields solving rates exceeding 29% for all models, whereas mathematical formalism falls below 12% for most.
The specific knowledge domain and type significantly influence how models acquire and apply contextual knowledge.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F10" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.03587v1/overview_solverate_reason_page1.svg" id="A2.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:494/792;" width="494" height="792"></object>

For other models, we use their reasoning variants.
</figcaption>
</figure>

<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Impact of Reasoning on Context Learning</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we present the performance comparison of nine frontier LMs under different reasoning effort settings, as shown in Figure <a href="#A3.F14" title="Figure 14 ‣ Appendix C Impact of Reasoning on Context Learning ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> and Figure <a href="#A3.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ Appendix C Impact of Reasoning on Context Learning ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>.
For models with adjustable reasoning effort (GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, and Gemini-3-Pro), we compare their highest and lowest settings.
For other models, we compare their reasoning and non-reasoning variants.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Results show that for the majority of models, higher reasoning effort facilitates more effective context learning.
Kimi-K2 exhibits the most significant improvement, with an average performance gap of 5.7% between the two reasoning settings.
However, for a few models, increasing reasoning effort does not improve context learning performance.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.F14" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.03587v1/overview_reason_comparison_page1.svg" id="A3.F14.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:494/631;" width="494" height="631"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 14: </span>
Comparison of model performance under different reasoning effort settings (Part 1/2).
For most models, higher reasoning effort leads to more effective context learning.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A3.F15" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.03587v1/overview_reason_comparison_page2.svg" id="A3.F15.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:494/792;" width="494" height="792"></object>

<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Impact of Context and Input Length on Context Learning</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we analyze how context and input length affect model performance on CL-bench, as shown in Figure <a href="#A4.F16" title="Figure 16 ‣ Appendix D Impact of Context and Input Length on Context Learning ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a> and Figure <a href="#A4.F17" title="Figure 17 ‣ Appendix D Impact of Context and Input Length on Context Learning ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The two figures exhibit nearly identical trends.
This is expected, as model input consists of system prompt, context, and a specific task, with context constituting the dominant proportion of total input length.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">All models exhibit consistent performance degradation as context length increases, regardless of reasoning effort.
For most models, solving rates drop from approximately 25-35% at 0-4K tokens to 5-10% at 32K+ tokens.
Longer contexts pose greater challenges for context learning, both because learning and applying knowledge from extensive material is inherently more difficult, and because models may be limited by their long-context reasoning capabilities.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Additionally, the advantage of higher reasoning effort becomes more pronounced with longer contexts.
At shorter context lengths (0-4K), the performance gap between high and low reasoning effort is often minimal.
However, at longer context lengths, more models benefit significantly from higher reasoning effort.
GPT-5.1 shows the most robust performance on long contexts, maintaining a solving rate of 16.2% at 32K+ tokens, substantially higher than other LMs.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.F16" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.03587v1/overview_context_token_length.svg" id="A4.F16.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:494/405;" width="494" height="405"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 16: </span>
Model performance across different context length ranges under different reasoning effort settings.
Longer contexts pose greater challenges for context learning, and the advantage of higher reasoning effort becomes more pronounced as context length increases.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A4.F17" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.03587v1/overview_input_token_length.svg" id="A4.F17.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:494/405;" width="494" height="405"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 17: </span>
Model performance across different input length ranges under different reasoning effort settings. The trend is consistent with that of context length (Figure <a href="#A4.F16" title="Figure 16 ‣ Appendix D Impact of Context and Input Length on Context Learning ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a>), as context constitutes the dominant proportion of total input.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>System Prompt for the LM-based Verifier</h2>

<div id="A5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present the system prompt used by the LM-based verifier to grade model solutions in Table <a href="#A5.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ Appendix E System Prompt for the LM-based Verifier ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span>System prompt used by the LM-based verifier to enforce strict rubric adherence.</figcaption>
<table id="A5.T4.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="A5.T4.2.1" class="ltx_tr" style="--ltx-bg-color:#ECECEC;">
<td id="A5.T4.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_align_top ltx_border_tt"><span id="A5.T4.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">System Prompt: LM-based Verifier</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A5.T4.2.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A5.T4.2.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A5.T4.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:389.5pt;">
<span id="A5.T4.2.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Starting now, you are a rigorous instruction-following grading teacher. Your task is to accurately grade and score student answers based on the <span id="A5.T4.2.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">[Rubrics]</span>.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A5.T4.2.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A5.T4.2.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top" style="padding-bottom: 2.0pt;"></td></tr>
<tr id="A5.T4.2.4" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A5.T4.2.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A5.T4.2.4.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:389.5pt;">
<span id="A5.T4.2.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.T4.2.4.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Grading criteria (binary).</span> This is a strict, all-or-nothing grading system. The final score is binary. 
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A5.T4.2.4.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Score = 1:</span> the student’s answer must perfectly satisfy every single requirement listed in the <span id="A5.T4.2.4.1.1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">[Rubrics]</span>. 
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A5.T4.2.4.1.1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Score = 0:</span> if even one requirement is not fully met.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A5.T4.2.5" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A5.T4.2.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top" style="padding-bottom: 2.0pt;"></td></tr>
<tr id="A5.T4.2.6" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A5.T4.2.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A5.T4.2.6.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:389.5pt;">
<span id="A5.T4.2.6.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.T4.2.6.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Grading process.</span> Please strictly follow the steps below for analysis—no steps may be skipped. 
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A5.T4.2.6.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Step 1: Analyze the Standard Answer.</span> 
<br class="ltx_break"> List all explicit requirements in the <span id="A5.T4.2.6.1.1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">[Rubrics]</span> item by item (format, content, quantity, order, etc.). 
<br class="ltx_break"> Identify implicit requirements in the <span id="A5.T4.2.6.1.1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">[Rubrics]</span> (e.g., language style, logical structure). 
<br class="ltx_break"> Define specific evaluation criteria for each requirement (e.g., “must include X”, “must not exceed Y”). 
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A5.T4.2.6.1.1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Step 2: Check Each Requirement Against the Student’s Answer.</span> 
<br class="ltx_break"> For every requirement in the <span id="A5.T4.2.6.1.1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">[Rubrics]</span>, verify one by one whether the student’s answer fully satisfies it. 
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A5.T4.2.6.1.1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Step 3: Self-Reflection.</span> 
<br class="ltx_break"> <span id="A5.T4.2.6.1.1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Completeness Check:</span> all requirements reviewed with no omissions. 
<br class="ltx_break"> <span id="A5.T4.2.6.1.1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Strictness Check:</span> adhere to “fully satisfied” without subjective relaxation. 
<br class="ltx_break"> <span id="A5.T4.2.6.1.1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Consistency Check:</span> rationale aligns logically with the final score. 
<br class="ltx_break"> <span id="A5.T4.2.6.1.1.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Objectivity Check:</span> judgments based on objective facts rather than speculation.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A5.T4.2.7" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A5.T4.2.7.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top" style="padding-bottom: 2.0pt;"></td></tr>
<tr id="A5.T4.2.8" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A5.T4.2.8.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A5.T4.2.8.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:389.5pt;">
<span id="A5.T4.2.8.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.T4.2.8.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Output format requirements.</span> 
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A5.T4.2.8.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">[Grading Rationale]</span>: xxx 
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A5.T4.2.8.1.1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">[List of Requirement Satisfaction Status]</span>: <math id="A5.T4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}]</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A5.T4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> is the total number of requirements in the <span id="A5.T4.2.8.1.1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">[Rubrics]</span>, and <math id="A5.T4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> indicates whether the student’s answer meets the <math id="A5.T4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th requirement, with values "yes"/"no". 
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A5.T4.2.8.1.1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">[Overall Score]</span>: <math id="A5.T4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> points, where <math id="A5.T4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\in\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\in\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math>.</span>
</span></td></tr>

<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>In-depth Analysis of Context Learning Successes and Failures</h2>

<div id="A6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we present additional qualitative case studies following the style of Section <a href="#S5.SS1" title="5.1 Qualitative Analysis ‣ 5 Further Analysis ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.1</span></a>. Combined with the one analyzed in the main paper, we examine a total of 16 cases (4 per category) to illustrate the diverse performance of frontier language models.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Tables <a href="#A6.T12" title="Table 12 ‣ F.3 Rule System Application ‣ Appendix F In-depth Analysis of Context Learning Successes and Failures ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>, <a href="#A6.T14" title="Table 14 ‣ F.3 Rule System Application ‣ Appendix F In-depth Analysis of Context Learning Successes and Failures ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>, <a href="#A6.T17" title="Table 17 ‣ F.4 Domain Knowledge Reasoning ‣ Appendix F In-depth Analysis of Context Learning Successes and Failures ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a>, and <a href="#A6.T18" title="Table 18 ‣ F.4 Domain Knowledge Reasoning ‣ Appendix F In-depth Analysis of Context Learning Successes and Failures ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a> are cases where Gemini-3-Pro did not address the tasks correctly.
Tables <a href="#A6.T15" title="Table 15 ‣ F.3 Rule System Application ‣ Appendix F In-depth Analysis of Context Learning Successes and Failures ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a> shows a successful example that Gemini-3-Pro extracts combinatorial reasoning from a video transcript and correctly explains the formula 2×21×13+1=547 by justifying each factor’s role.
GPT series model generations can be found in Tables <a href="#A6.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ F.1 Empirical Discovery &amp; Simulation ‣ Appendix F In-depth Analysis of Context Learning Successes and Failures ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, <a href="#A6.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ F.1 Empirical Discovery &amp; Simulation ‣ Appendix F In-depth Analysis of Context Learning Successes and Failures ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, <a href="#A6.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ F.2 Procedural Task Execution ‣ Appendix F In-depth Analysis of Context Learning Successes and Failures ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>, <a href="#A6.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ F.2 Procedural Task Execution ‣ Appendix F In-depth Analysis of Context Learning Successes and Failures ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, <a href="#A6.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ F.2 Procedural Task Execution ‣ Appendix F In-depth Analysis of Context Learning Successes and Failures ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>, <a href="#A6.T13" title="Table 13 ‣ F.3 Rule System Application ‣ Appendix F In-depth Analysis of Context Learning Successes and Failures ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> and <a href="#A6.T16" title="Table 16 ‣ F.4 Domain Knowledge Reasoning ‣ Appendix F In-depth Analysis of Context Learning Successes and Failures ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a>.
We primarily focus on its failure cases to explore the capability boundaries of current frontier models.
A common pattern emerges across these failures: models demonstrate partial compliance by correctly handling explicit, surface-level requirements (e.g., formatting constraints in Table <a href="#A6.T13" title="Table 13 ‣ F.3 Rule System Application ‣ Appendix F In-depth Analysis of Context Learning Successes and Failures ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>, individual scheduling rules in Table <a href="#A6.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ F.2 Procedural Task Execution ‣ Appendix F In-depth Analysis of Context Learning Successes and Failures ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, basic document identification in Table <a href="#A6.T16" title="Table 16 ‣ F.4 Domain Knowledge Reasoning ‣ Appendix F In-depth Analysis of Context Learning Successes and Failures ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a>), yet systematically fail when tasks demand deeper reasoning.
For Table <a href="#A6.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ F.2 Procedural Task Execution ‣ Appendix F In-depth Analysis of Context Learning Successes and Failures ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>, we present a case where the model correctly refuses the prohibited request but fails to fulfill the subsequent task requirements, providing only conceptual guidance instead of a complete compliant solution. Tables <a href="#A6.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ F.1 Empirical Discovery &amp; Simulation ‣ Appendix F In-depth Analysis of Context Learning Successes and Failures ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> and <a href="#A6.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ F.2 Procedural Task Execution ‣ Appendix F In-depth Analysis of Context Learning Successes and Failures ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> demonstrate that the model can produce substantively correct reasoning while still violating strict procedural requirements.
In Tables <a href="#A6.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ F.1 Empirical Discovery &amp; Simulation ‣ Appendix F In-depth Analysis of Context Learning Successes and Failures ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> and <a href="#A6.T19" title="Table 19 ‣ F.4 Domain Knowledge Reasoning ‣ Appendix F In-depth Analysis of Context Learning Successes and Failures ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a>, we present a Kimi-K2-Thinking success case that satisfies all grading criteria for context-dependent simulation initialization, and a failure case where the model provides accurate historical context but fails due to violations of strict formatting requirements. In Table <a href="#A6.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ F.1 Empirical Discovery &amp; Simulation ‣ Appendix F In-depth Analysis of Context Learning Successes and Failures ‣ CL-bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, we also present a Doubao-1.6-Thinking failure case where the model captures constants, but misses required variants and violates list-format rules in pattern-discovery.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">These qualitative analyses corroborate the findings presented in our main paper: frontier LMs continue to neglect or misapply contextual information, resulting in erroneous solutions.
Moreover, inherent limitations in long-context reasoning and instruction following further exacerbate failures in in-context learning.
Taken together, these results show the necessity for LMs to develop stronger capabilities for efficiently learning from and applying novel contextual knowledge, enhancing their practical applicability.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<section id="A6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.1 </span>Empirical Discovery &amp; Simulation</h3>

<figure id="A6.T5" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span>
In this example, GPT-5.2 computes the correct electron entry angle from helical motion data.
Nevertheless, it does not explain the rationale for the assumed magnetic-field orientation or specify the units of the position variables, illustrating how large language models can produce correct numerical results while lacking logical transparency and adherence to scientific conventions.

<span id="A6.T5.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:397.5pt;">
<span id="A6.T5.2.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.T5.2.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">System Prompt</span></span>

<tr id="A6.T5.2.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A6.T5.2.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb">
<span id="A6.T5.2.3.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:397.5pt;">
<span id="A6.T5.2.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">You are an expert assistant in reverse-engineering models. Your purpose is to ingest raw data and deduce underlying mathematical equations, governing physics or physical constants behind it. Above all, you prioritise parsimony and apply Occam’s Razor whenever possible.</span>
<span id="A6.T5.2.3.1.1.2" class="ltx_p">If the user explicitly names or a mode of operation, you must use that mode regardless of data context. If no mode is explicitly named, you must infer the mode based on the “Trigger” criteria specified below. You have 3 key modes of operation:</span>
<span id="A6.T5.2.3.1.1.3" class="ltx_p">MODE: REGRESSION MODELLING</span>
<span id="A6.T5.2.3.1.1.4" class="ltx_p">…(Irrelevant lines omitted)</span>
<span id="A6.T5.2.3.1.1.5" class="ltx_p">MODE: PARAMETER TUNING</span>
<span id="A6.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<span id="A6.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<span id="A6.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A6.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Function: extracting underlying constants and coefficients only from raw data;</span>
</span></span>
<span id="A6.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<span id="A6.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A6.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Trigger: the user provides raw data with context (e.g. either an implied or explicitly defined model) and/or requests the value of a parameter in any way;</span>
</span></span>
<span id="A6.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<span id="A6.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A6.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Action: accept the given model and solve for coefficients and parameters (e.g. decay rate, initial temperature);</span>
</span></span>
<span id="A6.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<span id="A6.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A6.I2.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Constraint: do not suggest alternative models; focus on finding the parameter values as closely as possible.</span>
</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A6.T5.2.3.1.1.6" class="ltx_p">MODE: REPLICATION</span>
<span id="A6.T5.2.3.1.1.7" class="ltx_p">…(Irrelevant lines omitted)</span>
<span id="A6.T5.2.3.1.1.8" class="ltx_p">Your responses will always:</span>
<span id="A6.I3" class="ltx_itemize">
<span id="A6.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<span id="A6.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A6.I3.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Be justified, with brief rationale behind the mode selected and values or forms derived;</span>
</span></span>
<span id="A6.I3.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<span id="A6.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A6.I3.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Have zero conversational filler, with no introductions (e.g. “Sure, I can help you with that!”) or casual conclusions (e.g. “I hope you find this analysis helpful!”);</span>
</span></span>
<span id="A6.I3.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<span id="A6.I3.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A6.I3.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Render all mathematical variables, constants and equations in LaTeX for maximum readability, with display maths ($$…$$) for final governing equations or model definitions and inline maths ($…$) for variables, constants, units and explanatory equations;</span>
</span></span>
<span id="A6.I3.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<span id="A6.I3.i4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A6.I3.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Have the first line “MODE: mode triggered”;</span>
</span></span>
<span id="A6.I3.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<span id="A6.I3.i5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A6.I3.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Obey the following operational heuristics:</span>
<span id="A6.I3.i5.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<span id="A6.I3.i5.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="A6.I3.i5.I1.i1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">–</span></span> 
<span id="A6.I3.i5.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A6.I3.i5.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Hierarchy of simplicity: if two models fit with similar error margins ( 5%), prefer the model higher up the hierarchy of linear, power law/monomial…</span>

<span id="A6.I3.i5.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="A6.I3.i5.I1.i2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">–</span></span>

<span id="A6.I3.i5.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Noise tolerance: if data appears noisy, do not attempt to fit a high-order polynomial…</span>

<span id="A6.SS1.tab1.1.3.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:397.5pt;">
<span id="A6.SS1.tab1.1.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS1.tab1.1.3.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model Generated Solution</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A6.SS1.tab1.1.4" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A6.SS1.tab1.1.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb">
<span id="A6.SS1.tab1.1.4.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:397.5pt;">
<span id="A6.SS1.tab1.1.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">MODE: PARAMETER TUNING</span>
<span id="A6.SS1.tab1.1.4.1.1.2" class="ltx_p">Assumed model and rationale</span>
<span id="A6.SS1.tab1.1.4.1.1.3" class="ltx_p">Helical motion in a uniform magnetic field with <math id="A6.SS1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐁</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{B}</annotation></semantics></math> aligned along the <math id="A6.SS1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>-axis. The electron enters the field with velocity components split into:</span>
<span id="A6.I4" class="ltx_itemize">
<span id="A6.I4.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<span id="A6.I4.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A6.I4.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">parallel component <math id="A6.I4.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{\parallel}=v_{z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mo>∥</mo></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{\parallel}=v_{z}</annotation></semantics></math>,</span>
</span></span>
<span id="A6.I4.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<span id="A6.I4.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A6.I4.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">perpendicular component <math id="A6.I4.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{\perp}=\sqrt{v_{x}^{2}+v_{y}^{2}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mo>⟂</mo></msub><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><msubsup><mi>v</mi><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>v</mi><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{\perp}=\sqrt{v_{x}^{2}+v_{y}^{2}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</span>
</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A6.SS1.tab1.1.4.1.1.4" class="ltx_p">The pitch angle (entry angle relative to the magnetic field) is therefore</span>
<span id="A6.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<span><span class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<span class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></span>
<span class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A6.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{v_{\perp}}{v_{\parallel}}\right)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>tan</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>v</mi><mo>⟂</mo></msub><msub><mi>v</mi><mo>∥</mo></msub></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{v_{\perp}}{v_{\parallel}}\right).</annotation></semantics></math></span>
<span class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></span></span></span>
</span>
<span id="A6.SS1.tab1.1.4.1.1.5" class="ltx_p">Velocity extraction</span>
<span id="A6.SS1.tab1.1.4.1.1.6" class="ltx_p">Using the first nonzero timestep to estimate initial velocities:</span>
<span id="A6.I5" class="ltx_itemize">
<span id="A6.I5.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<span id="A6.I5.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A6.I5.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="A6.I5.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta t=1.43048254\times 10^{-11}\,\text{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>1.43048254</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>s</mtext></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta t=1.43048254\times 10^{-11}\,\text{s}</annotation></semantics></math></span>
</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A6.SS1.tab1.1.4.1.1.7" class="ltx_p">From the data:</span>
<span id="A6.I6" class="ltx_itemize">
<span id="A6.I6.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<span id="A6.I6.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A6.I6.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="A6.I6.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=6.49356982\times 10^{-5}\Rightarrow v_{x}\approx\frac{6.4936\times 10^{-5}}{1.4305\times 10^{-11}}\approx 4.54\times 10^{6}\,\text{m/s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>6.49356982</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⇒</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mo>≈</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>6.4936</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>1.4305</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>4.54</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>6</mn></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>m/s</mtext></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=6.49356982\times 10^{-5}\Rightarrow v_{x}\approx\frac{6.4936\times 10^{-5}}{1.4305\times 10^{-11}}\approx 4.54\times 10^{6}\,\text{m/s}</annotation></semantics></math></span>
</span></span>
<span id="A6.I6.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<span id="A6.I6.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A6.I6.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="A6.I6.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=8.16860393\times 10^{-7}\Rightarrow v_{y}\approx 5.71\times 10^{4}\,\text{m/s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>8.16860393</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⇒</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>5.71</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>m/s</mtext></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=8.16860393\times 10^{-7}\Rightarrow v_{y}\approx 5.71\times 10^{4}\,\text{m/s}</annotation></semantics></math></span>
</span></span>
<span id="A6.I6.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<span id="A6.I6.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A6.I6.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="A6.I6.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z=1.27456928\times 10^{-4}\Rightarrow v_{z}\approx 8.91\times 10^{6}\,\text{m/s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1.27456928</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⇒</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>8.91</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>6</mn></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>m/s</mtext></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z=1.27456928\times 10^{-4}\Rightarrow v_{z}\approx 8.91\times 10^{6}\,\text{m/s}</annotation></semantics></math></span>
</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A6.SS1.tab1.1.4.1.1.8" class="ltx_p">Thus:</span>
<span id="A6.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<span class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></span></span></span>
