<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:397.5pt;">
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Context (continued)</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:397.5pt;">
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">VORTIGERN.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1.2" class="ltx_p">Most gracious sov’reign! to command is thine,
And as a subject mine is to obey.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1.3" class="ltx_p">CONSTANTIUS.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1.4" class="ltx_p">Such was the answer we did here expect,
And farther now we shall explain our meaning;
As frozen age we find doth fast approach,
And state affairs lie heavy with ourself,
We here to thee half of our pow’r resign,
That thy reward may pace with this thy labour.
To this our proposition what reply?</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1.5" class="ltx_p">VORTIGERN.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1.6" class="ltx_p">Oh! my most noble, good, and bounteous lord,
These honours are indeed so great, so weighty,
I fear lest like a garment too confin’d,
They aukwardly should press upon the wearer.
Therefore, my gracious lord! let one more worthy,
I do beseech thee, bear them.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1.7" class="ltx_p">…(Remaining lines omitted)</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1.8" class="ltx_p">SCENE II. A Chamber in VORTIGERN’s Palace.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1.9" class="ltx_p">[Enter EDMUNDA and FLAVIA.]</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1.10" class="ltx_p">FLAVIA.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1.11" class="ltx_p">Dearest mother! why let watery grief
Like a corroding and slow malady
Nip thus the fairest and most beauteous pearl,
That ever art of man by stealth or cunning
Drew from the azure vault of brightest heav’n,
To grace this earth? —Oh! my beloved mother!
Turn, turn those tear worn eyes, and let one smile,
One cheering look of sweet serenity,
Beam forth to comfort my afflicted soul!</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1.12" class="ltx_p">EDMUNDA.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1.13" class="ltx_p">Oh! heavens! my gentle Flavia! would I could!
But this corroding pensive melancholy
Most venom like, destroys its nourisher.
Oh! Vortigern, my lov’d, once loving husband,
Why rend this bursting heart with cold disdain,
E’en the poor culprit brought before his judge
May boldly plead his cause; but I alas!
Most innocent, and ignorant of my fault,
Must bear the weight of judgment.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1.14" class="ltx_p">[Enter PASCENTIUS.]</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1.15" class="ltx_p">…(Remaining lines omitted)</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1.16" class="ltx_p">SCENE III. Another Apartment in VORTIGERN’s Palace.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1.17" class="ltx_p">[Enter VORTIGERN.]</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1.18" class="ltx_p">VORTIGERN.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1.19" class="ltx_p">Thus far, then have my deeds a sanction found,
For still each morn doth the resplendent sun
Dart forth its golden rays, to grace my sight.
O what an inconsistent thing is man!
There was a time when e’en the thought of murder
Would have congeal’d my very mass of blood;
"And, as a tree, on the approaching storm,
"E’en so my very frame would shake and tremble:"
But now I stand not at the act itself,
Which breaks all bonds of hospitality.—
To me, the King hath ever been most kind;
…</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1.20" class="ltx_p">[Enter Servant]</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1.21" class="ltx_p">SERVANT.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1.22" class="ltx_p">Two officers, my lord! await your leisure.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1.23" class="ltx_p">…(Remaining lines omitted)</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.2.1.1.24" class="ltx_p">END OF FIRST ACT.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.3.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:397.5pt;">
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.3.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model Generated Solution</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.4" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb">
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.4.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:397.5pt;">
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">What an excellent choice for dialogue practice! You’ve stumbled upon a fascinating piece of theatrical history with <span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.4.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Vortigern and Rowena</span>. This play is infamous as one of the great literary forgeries of the 18th century—written in 1796 by a young man named William Henry Ireland, who tried to pass it off as a newly discovered lost work of Shakespeare. The Drury Lane Theatre actually staged it briefly before scholars exposed it as a fake. The language is deliberately archaic and flows in blank verse, which makes it quite challenging indeed—perfect for stretching your club’s skills with complex syntax, heightened emotion, and rhythm.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.4.1.1.2" class="ltx_p">The entire play is solidly in the public domain, so you can work with it freely, and its heavy, dramatic speeches will give you wonderful material for exploring subtext, ambition, and moral conflict without needing any production elements.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.4.1.1.3" class="ltx_p">Now, looking carefully at Act I as you’ve shared it, here are the characters you’ll encounter:</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.4.1.1.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.4.1.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Characters who speak in Act I:</span></span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.4.1.1.5" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.4.1.1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Constantius</span> – The reigning King, who begins the act by offering Vortigern a share of his power. He appears serene and trusting, completely unaware of the betrayal being plotted against him.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.4.1.1.6" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.4.1.1.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Vortigern</span> – The central figure of the drama, whose hunger for absolute power drives the entire plot. He has by far the most stage time and delivers several major soliloquies wrestling with his conscience before committing to murder.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.4.1.1.7" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.tab7.1.4.1.1.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Pascentius</span> – Vortigern’s son, who brings news of his father’s new political position to his mother and sister. He seems youthful and earnest.</span>
</span></td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
<figure id="A6.SS4.tab8" class="ltx_table">
<table id="A6.SS4.tab8.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_tt">
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:397.5pt;">
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model Generated Solution (continued)</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:397.5pt;">
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Edmunda</span> – Vortigern’s wife (though in some historical versions she would be his mistress), who laments how ambition has stolen her husband from her. She speaks in deeply melancholy verse.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Flavia</span> – Vortigern’s daughter, devoted to her mother and secretly pledged to young Prince Aurelius. Her dialogue reveals both tenderness and growing alarm.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The Fool</span> – A whimsical, truth-telling character in the tradition of Shakespearean clowns. He speaks in witty, riddling prose and serves as a kind of moral barometer.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Two Murderers</span> – Hired assassins who debate the morality of their deed before ultimately killing Constantius. The second murderer has a crisis of conscience and fights his comrade.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.5" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A Servant</span> – Appears twice briefly to answer Vortigern’s summons.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.6" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">An Officer</span> – One of the guards who reports to Vortigern about the murdered King.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.7" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">First and Second Barons</span> – Representatives of the nobility who, after Constantius’s death, ask Vortigern to serve as Protector of the realm.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.8" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Characters who appear but remain silent:</span></span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.9" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Wortimerus</span> – Named in the opening scene but never speaks. He simply forms part of the court assembly.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.10" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.10.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Catagrius</span> – Similarly present in the first scene as part of the royal council, but has no lines.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.11" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.11.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Attendants</span> – General members of the court in Scene I who provide atmosphere but no dialogue.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.12" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.12.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A Groom</span> (also called a Page) – In Scene IV, he enters with Constantius, is given instructions to deliver a ring, and exits without speaking.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.13" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.13.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The remaining Guards</span> – In Scene V, only the Officer speaks; the other guards with Vortigern are silent.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.2.1.1.14" class="ltx_p">This first act is quite talk-heavy, which is perfect for your purposes. You’ll notice that characters frequently speak in extended monologues—Vortigern alone has five separate appearances where he delivers lengthy speeches. The Fool’s scenes offer a nice contrast with more playful, quick-witted exchanges, while the murder scene provides intense two-person dialogue with high stakes and emotional shifts. Even without staging the full narrative, these sections will give your club wonderful material for exploring how character motivation shapes speech patterns.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.3.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:397.5pt;">
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.3.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Rubrics</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.4" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.4.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:397.5pt;">
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">0. The response should use a friendly and supportive tone. For example, it should use phrases such as: "That’s a wonderful idea!" or "That’s a brilliant choice!"</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.4.1.1.2" class="ltx_p">1. The response should be conversational. For example, the response should use paragraphs and full sentences rather than numbered lists, bulleted lists, or tables.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.4.1.1.3" class="ltx_p">2. The response should identify all of the characters who have dialogue in the play as: Constantius, Vortigern, Edmunda, Flavia, Pascentius, Fool, Servant, First Murderer, Second Murderer, Officer, First Baron, Second Baron.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.4.1.1.4" class="ltx_p">3. The response should identify all of the characters who appear on stage, yet have no dialogue, as: Wortimerus, Catagrinus, Attendants, Guards, Groom/Page.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.4.1.1.5" class="ltx_p">4. The response should provide historical context for the play. For example, it could state that the play is a controversial work attributed to William Henry Ireland as a Shakespeare forgery from the 1790s.</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.4.1.1.6" class="ltx_p">5. The response should discuss the play’s suitability for practicing dialogue. For example, it could state: "Using it for dialogue practice is an excellent idea. The language is definitely archaic, which will be a great workout for your actors’ articulation and comprehension skills."</span>
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.4.1.1.7" class="ltx_p">6. The response should address the user’s observation about the play being old and the dialogue being difficult. For example, it should comment on the archaic language or blank verse style.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.5" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t">
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.5.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:397.5pt;">
<span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.tab8.1.5.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Discussion.</span>
This case evaluates Kimi-K2 on a context-dependent literary comprehension task that combines factual extraction with strict stylistic constraints.
The task requires identifying speaking and non-speaking characters in Act I of Vortigern and Rowena using the exact character names provided in the prompt, while maintaining a conversational, paragraph-based format.
Although the model correctly supplies historical context about William Henry Ireland’s Shakespeare forgery and explains the play’s usefulness for dialogue practice, it fails to meet all required conditions.
In particular, the response violates the formatting constraint by using lists instead of continuous prose, and it does not precisely follow the required character labels, misspelling Catagrinus as Catagrius.
This error illustrates a limitation in fine-grained instruction following.</span>
</span></td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<figure id="A6.SS4.tab9" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 20: </span>
This case compares two task types. The first is a Legal &amp; Regulatory extraction task that requires faithful, quote-accurate answers drawn only from a real appellate opinion; the second is a Legal Advisory task that requires applying a fictional criminal code with strict role and formatting constraints. The contrast highlights how one task is evidence-text driven with minimal inference, while the other is rule-driven with mandatory section-based reasoning and a verdict-first structure.
</figcaption>
<table id="A6.SS4.tab9.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="A6.SS4.tab9.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A6.SS4.tab9.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_tt">
<span id="A6.SS4.tab9.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:397.5pt;">
<span id="A6.SS4.tab9.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.tab9.1.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Case 1: Task Information</span></span>
<span id="A6.I39" class="ltx_itemize">
<span id="A6.I39.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<span id="A6.I39.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A6.I39.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">uid: dc91ab32-2885-4b6f-bd89-74bd1002183d</span>
</span></span>
<span id="A6.I39.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span>

<span id="A6.I39.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span>

<span id="A6.I39.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Task: Questions:</span>
</span>
<span id="A6.I39.i3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A6.I39.i3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">What exact legal rule does the court state governs when the statute of limitations begins to run for naturalization fraud? Quote the sentence that establishes it.</span>
</span>
<span id="A6.I39.i3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A6.I39.i3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">What specific immigration consequences does the opinion say Palmer’s counsel failed to advise him about?</span>

<span id="A6.I39.i3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">

</span></span>
</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A6.SS4.tab9.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A6.SS4.tab9.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A6.SS4.tab9.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:397.5pt;">
<span id="A6.SS4.tab9.1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.tab9.1.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Case 1: System Prompt</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A6.SS4.tab9.1.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A6.SS4.tab9.1.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A6.SS4.tab9.1.3.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:397.5pt;">
<span id="A6.SS4.tab9.1.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">You are ParalegalAI, a reliable legal research and drafting assistant who supports attorneys by summarizing legal materials, identifying relevant issues, locating controlling authorities, and producing well-structured drafts while never giving legal advice. You must follow instructions precisely, use only real and verifiable cases, statutes, and sources, and never fabricate citations or quotes. When analyzing excerpts, limit yourself to the text provided and answer “Not stated” if the information is absent. Maintain a professional, neutral tone; describe legal concepts objectively; and clearly explain your reasoning unless told otherwise. Ask clarifying questions only when necessary, and ensure all documents you draft follow appropriate conventions and include a note that attorney review is required.</span>
